title: Const Correctness and constexpr
relevance: Interviewers use const/constexpr to test whether candidates can write immutable API contracts, read pointer declarations correctly, and distinguish runtime immutability from compile-time evaluation.

phases.goal: Establish what const means, how to read const pointer declarations, and why const references are the default for large inputs.

must_hit.point: A const variable must be initialised at declaration because it can never be assigned to later.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says the compiler rejects later assignment; initialisation is mandatory.

must_hit.point: Right-to-left reading: start at the variable name and read backwards so each const and * binds to the token on its right.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks a declaration like const int* p or int* const p from the name outward.

must_hit.point: const int* (or int const*) is pointer-to-const: the pointer may reseat, but the pointee cannot be modified through it.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States reseating is OK and *p assignment is an error; notes the two spellings are equivalent.

must_hit.point: int* const is a const pointer: the address is fixed and must be initialised, but the pointee may be modified.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says *p write is OK and reseating the pointer is an error.

must_hit.point: const T& aliases without copying and forbids modification—the efficient idiom for passing large objects.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions no copy plus cannot mutate; contrasts with pass-by-value safety and pass-by-reference cost.

probes: How do you read const int* versus int* const, and what mutation does each forbid?
Why pass a large string as const std::string& instead of by value?

hints.1: Think about which part is immutable: the pointer address or the data it points to.
hints.2: Read the declaration right-to-left from the name; then contrast pointer-to-const with const-pointer.
hints.3: const int* protects the int; int* const protects the pointer; const T& gives reference performance without allowing writes.

phases.goal: Explain const member functions, mutable, const parameters/returns, and how constexpr variables and functions evaluate.

must_hit.point: const after a member function means it does not modify the object's observable state; this becomes const ClassName* const.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions trailing const, enforcement by the compiler, and the const this pointer.

must_hit.point: mutable lets a member change inside a const member function for bookkeeping that does not alter logical external state.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives caching, access counts, or mutexes as the usual reason for the escape hatch.

must_hit.point: const on a by-value parameter only freezes the callee's local copy and does not affect the caller.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says it is an implementation detail; caller-visible interface is unchanged.

must_hit.point: Returning const T& exposes internal data without a copy and without letting the caller modify it; returning a const value by value is generally obsolete and inhibits move semantics.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Prefers const reference getters; notes const-by-value return is outdated in modern C++.

must_hit.point: constexpr means the value is known at compile time; a constexpr variable must be initialised with a constant expression.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts with runtime input; rejects initialising constexpr from a non-constant like cin input.

must_hit.point: A constexpr function can run at compile time when arguments are constant expressions, and falls back to run time otherwise.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives compile-time call with a literal argument versus runtime call with a non-constant variable.

probes: What does const after a member function mean, and how does mutable fit?
When does a constexpr function run at compile time versus run time?

hints.1: Trailing const is a promise about the object; constexpr is about when the value is known.
hints.2: Describe this inside a const method, then the compile-time-if-possible rule for constexpr functions.
hints.3: this is const ClassName* const; mutable is for non-logical state; constexpr functions evaluate at compile time only with constant-expression arguments.

phases.goal: Contrast const versus constexpr, consteval, constinit, and the API versus optimisation motives for const-correctness.

must_hit.point: const is runtime immutability after initialisation; constexpr requires full compile-time evaluability; all constexpr variables are implicitly const, but not all const variables are constexpr.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both directions of the implication clearly: constexpr ⇒ const, not the reverse.

must_hit.point: Const-correctness serves API contracts (e.g. const Widget& means read-only) and enables more aggressive compiler optimisations when values cannot change.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names both intent communication and optimisation of registers/memory accesses.

must_hit.point: Since C++17, constexpr variables are implicitly inline, so they can be defined in headers without multiple-definition errors (historically addressed with inline).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions C++17 implicit inline and safe header definitions across translation units.

must_hit.point: consteval (C++20) must evaluate at compile time; constexpr only can. constinit (C++20) forces compile-time initialisation with static/thread storage without making the variable immutable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates mandatory compile-time functions from constexpr's optional path, and constinit from const.

probes: What is the difference between const and constexpr?
How do consteval and constinit differ from constexpr?

hints.1: One is about not changing later; the other is about knowing the value during compilation.
hints.2: Map const → runtime immutability, constexpr → may be compile-time, consteval → must be, constinit → init-only constraint.
hints.3: constexpr variables are const; consteval is an immediate function; constinit avoids static-init-order issues without immutability.

phases.goal: Apply const-correctness propagation and choose the right const/constexpr tool in APIs and headers.

must_hit.point: Const-correctness must propagate: a const object may only be passed to const parameters or have its const member functions called.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes the outward propagation rule and what you can legally do with a const object.

must_hit.point: Prefer const T& for large read-only parameters and const T& getters for cheap read-only exposure of members.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Applies the printMessage(const std::string&) and Config::getName() patterns.

must_hit.point: Use constexpr for true compile-time constants and header-safe shared constants; use consteval when evaluation must be compile-time; use constinit when only initialisation must be compile-time.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Picks the tool by whether immutability, optional compile-time eval, mandatory eval, or init-only is required.

probes: If you hold a const object, what are you allowed to call or pass it to?
When would you put constexpr in a header versus use consteval or constinit?

hints.1: Const spreads through the API surface—what happens if one layer forgets const?
hints.2: Start from a const object and list legal calls; then match constexpr/consteval/constinit to the need.
hints.3: Only const methods/parameters; constexpr in headers is implicitly inline since C++17; consteval requires compile-time; constinit initialises without freezing later writes.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: const promises the object will not be modified after initialisation (runtime immutability). constexpr requires the value to be fully evaluable at compile time. Every constexpr variable is implicitly const; a const variable need not be constexpr.
const int* / int const* protects the pointee (pointer may reseat). int* const protects the pointer address (pointee may change). const int* const freezes both.

tradeoffs.topic: const by-value return vs const T& return
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Returning const by value is generally obsolete in modern C++ and inhibits move semantics. Returning const T& is the common way to expose internal data without copying or allowing modification.

constexpr functions can run at compile time or fall back to run time. consteval (C++20) must run at compile time. constinit (C++20) demands compile-time initialisation for static/thread storage without making the variable immutable.

tradeoffs.topic: constexpr vs historical inline for header constants
tradeoffs.strong_answer: inline was historically used to avoid multiple-definition errors for header variables. Since C++17, constexpr variables are implicitly inline and can be defined directly in headers safely.

gotchas.trap: Treating const int* and int* const as the same.
gotchas.correction: They differ: const int* protects the data; int* const protects the pointer address.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a constexpr function always runs at compile time.
gotchas.correction: It runs at compile time only with constant-expression arguments; otherwise it falls back to run time.

gotchas.trap: Thinking const after a member function is only documentation.
gotchas.correction: The compiler enforces it: this becomes const ClassName* const, and non-mutable members cannot be modified.

gotchas.trap: Returning const by value from accessors in modern C++.
gotchas.correction: That pattern is generally obsolete and inhibits move semantics; prefer returning const T& when exposing members read-only.

gotchas.trap: Assuming every const variable is a compile-time constant.
gotchas.correction: const is runtime immutability; only constexpr (or consteval for functions) requires compile-time evaluability. All constexpr variables are const, not vice versa.
